page_title: Email and Messages - Digital Confidence Centre
title: Email and Messages
description: Send emails and texts safely, spot scam messages, share photos with family, and block unwanted callers. Free, plain-language lesson for Canadian seniors. No account needed.
lesson_time: About 12 minutes, at your own pace
lead: How to send emails and texts safely, spot scam messages, and share photos with the people you love.

story.label: Rose's story
paragraphs: Rose, 71, loves getting emails from her grandchildren: photos of the kids, funny stories about school, weekend plans. But she also receives about 30 unwanted emails a day, and for a long time she was afraid to open any of them in case one carried a virus.

Once Rose learned what to look for, everything changed. Now she sorts through her inbox every morning, keeps the messages she wants, and deletes the rest, without a moment of worry. Most of those scary emails, she says, are just like junk mail in your real mailbox: annoying, but harmless as long as you throw them away.

coach: Email can feel like a place where one wrong tap ruins everything. It is not. Reading an email cannot harm your device, and deleting the wrong one is almost always undoable. The only real skill is learning to pause before you tap a link, and by the end of this page that pause will feel natural.

sections.text: Your device comes with an email app: Mail on an iPad or iPhone, Gmail on most Android devices. Whichever you use, it works like a set of mailboxes at the post office:

items: Sent: copies of emails you have sent, so you can look back at them.
Drafts: emails you started writing but have not sent yet.
Junk or Spam: mail your device thinks is junk. Check it now and then, as a real message can land here by mistake.
Trash or Bin: emails you have deleted. They wait here for a while before being removed for good, so you can recover one if you delete it by accident.

sections.label: If your inbox feels full
sections.text: You do not need to read every single email. Focus on messages from people you know. You can always delete the rest, just like tossing junk mail from your letterbox into the recycling.

sections.title: Writing and sending an email
steps: Open your email app (Mail on Apple, Gmail on Android).
Look for a pencil or compose button, usually in a corner. Tap it to start a new email.
In the To field, type the email address of the person you are writing to.
Tap the Subject field and type a short description, for example "Sunday dinner plans".
Tap the large blank area and type your message.
When you are done, tap the send button (an upward arrow or a paper plane).

sections.label: Confidence check
sections.text: You can write and send an email. That is a powerful skill for staying connected with the people you love. Before sending, take one moment to check the address in the To field, so your message reaches the right person.
A scam email is designed to look real and to make you act quickly. Here is a simple check to run on any message from someone you do not recognise.

sections.title: The email safety check
steps: Check the sender. Tap the sender's name to see the full address. Does it look right? ("rbc.com" is real; "rbc-alerts-canada.com" is fake.)
Look for urgency. "Act now!" or "Your account will be closed!" Real companies give you time.
Check the greeting. "Dear Customer" is a red flag. Your bank knows your name.
Do not tap the links. If you must check, press and hold a link to preview where it really goes.
When in doubt, delete it. If a real company needs you, they will contact you another way.

sections.label: Watch out
sections.text: Never tap a link in an email that asks you to "verify your account" or "confirm your identity". Legitimate companies do not ask you to do this by email. If you are unsure, open your browser and go to the company's website directly.

steps.name: Stop
steps.text: Do not tap any links in an unexpected email.

steps.name: Breathe
steps.text: No real company will close your account because you took a few minutes to think.

steps.name: Verify
steps.text: Go to the company's website yourself, or call the number on your bank card.

sections.text: Opening a PDF? Watch for fake "install this" prompts

A PDF is just a document, like a letter or a form, saved so it looks the same on every device. Most web browsers today open a PDF right in a new tab, with nothing to download or install. If a website suddenly tells you that you need to install a special "viewer" or "player" before you can see a document, that is a warning sign, not a normal step.

sections.label: Tip
sections.text: Adobe Acrobat Reader is a real, well-known program for opening PDFs, and it is safe to install if you get it directly from adobe.com. But you almost never need it. Your browser (Safari, Chrome, or Edge) already opens PDFs on its own, with no extra software required.

sections.label: Watch out
sections.text: If a pop-up says you must install something before you can view a document, do not click it. Close the tab instead. If you were trying to reach a real organisation, like your bank or the government, open your browser and go to their website directly.
Getting calls from unknown numbers or annoying text messages? You can block them, and you can always unblock them later if you change your mind.

sections.title: Blocking a phone number
steps: Open the Phone app and tap Recents to see your call history.
Find the number you want to block.
On an iPhone, tap the small "i" next to it; on Android, press and hold the number.
Choose Block this caller or Block number.
Confirm. That number can no longer call or text you.

sections.title: Sending a photo by text message
steps: Open the Messages app and open a conversation with the person you want to send the photo to.
Look for the + button or the camera or photo icon near where you type.
Tap Photos and choose the picture you want to send.
Tap the send arrow. Your photo is on its way.

sections.label: The move is
sections.text: Read freely, because reading an email cannot harm you. Before you tap any link or install anything, pause and ask whether you expected this message. When in doubt, delete it and go to the company's website yourself.

sections.heading: Quick check: test your knowledge
sections.intro: Tap the answer you think is correct. There is no score kept and nothing to sign in to.

options: Unwanted email, usually trying to sell something or scam you
questions.right: Right. Spam is unwanted email sent in bulk, from harmless advertising to dangerous scams. Your app filters most of it into a junk folder.
questions.wrong: Not quite. Spam is unwanted email sent in bulk, ranging from advertising to scams. Most of it lands in your junk folder automatically.

questions.q: 2. An email asks you to click a link to "verify your account". The safest response is:
options: Click the link, it is probably your bank
Do not click, go to your account through the official website or app yourself
Reply to ask if it is real
questions.right: Exactly. Always reach your bank through its official app or website, never through a link in an email.
questions.wrong: The safest step is to go to your bank's official app or website yourself. Scammers build convincing fake login pages behind those links.

questions.q: 3. You get a text from an unknown number with a link. You should:
options: Tap the link to find out what it is
Delete the message and do not tap any links from unknown senders
Reply to ask who sent it
questions.right: Perfect. Never tap links from unknown senders. Delete the message and move on.
questions.wrong: The safe move is to delete it. Never tap links from senders you do not know, even if the message looks urgent.

sections.heading: Your progress
sections.intro: Tick each item as you feel confident with it. This is saved on this device only, with no account needed.
items: I can find my inbox, sent, and junk folders
I can write and send an email
I can run the email safety check on a message I do not recognise
I know not to install a "viewer" just to open a document
I can block an unwanted caller

success_state: Well done. You can now send and receive messages, spot the signs of a scam, and share photos with family. Your inbox is working for you, not against you.
